planting.note: Plant head-end tuber setts 4-6 inches deep once soil is reliably warm, in deep, loose, well-drained soil mounded or ridged; set a sturdy 8-10 foot trellis right away since the twining vines grow quickly.

directions: St. Vincent is a long-cultivated Jamaican strain of water yam grown under several local sub-names, including Moonshine, Darknight, and Purple, which differ mainly in flesh color and are distinguished from one another by growers through folk tradition as much as formal classification. Set tuber head pieces into deep, fertile, well-worked soil and provide tall support immediately, since the vigorous vines climb fast and become heavy with foliage. Keep soil evenly moist through the long warm growing season and taper off watering as the vines yellow near harvest, roughly nine to eleven months after planting. Cure harvested tubers in a shaded, well-ventilated spot before storage to improve keeping quality.
sources: Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI)
Jamaica Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries

planting.note: Plant tuber head setts in deep, friable, well-drained soil once it has warmed past the last frost, mounding rows to ease later harvest, and trellis the vines from the start.

directions: Renta, also marketed as Barbados yam, is a named water yam type grown across Jamaica and the Eastern Caribbean and valued as a finer-textured, more delicate specialty yam than bulk commodity types. Starch researchers have noted that Renta's tuber starch forms distinctively triangular granules rather than the rounder shapes typical of most other water yam cultivars, a trait tied to its notably smooth, dense-cooking flesh. Grow it on a tall trellis in full sun with consistently moist, fertile soil through the long tropical growing season, reducing water as foliage yellows near maturity. Harvest carefully to avoid bruising the tubers, which are prized for boiling, roasting, and festival-style preparations.
sources: Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI)
Jamaica Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries

planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots or tissue-cultured palms in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; fruit set is reliable only with a nearby male pollinator or hand pollination.

directions: Samany is one of Egypt's leading soft date cultivars, grown widely in the Nile Delta and Fayoum Oasis for a large, plump fruit with reddish-spotted skin and a notably high pulp-to-fruit ratio. Unlike Egypt's crisp, fresh-eaten Zaghloul, Samany is typically left to ripen further and is enjoyed soft and very sweet, either fresh or lightly dried. As with all date palms, it needs a long, hot growing season, deep well-drained soil, and dependable pollination to bear well, with many years of growth required before a young palm reaches bearing age. Plan for a long-term planting with ample overhead and root room.
sources: FAO Regional Office for the Near East — Date Palm Cultivars
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Date Palm Culture

planting.note: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured palms in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; needs a long hot season and either a male pollinator nearby or hand pollination to fruit reliably.

directions: Bint Aisha, meaning 'daughter of Aisha' in Arabic, is a traditional Egyptian soft date cultivar recognized by its comparatively small, scarlet-red fruit, a color that sets it apart from the more amber or maroon tones of other popular Egyptian soft dates. It is grown in oasis and Delta plantings and typically harvested and eaten at the crisp khalal or soft rutab stage rather than fully dried. Give it the same long, hot growing season, deep well-drained soil, and dependable pollination that all commercial date cultivars require, and expect many years of growth before a young palm reaches bearing maturity. Site it with plenty of permanent room to spread as it matures into a large specimen.
sources: FAO Regional Office for the Near East — Date Palm Cultivars
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Date Palm Culture

planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and a long, very hot season; a male pollinator or hand pollination is needed for consistent fruit set.

directions: Sakkoti is a classic Egyptian dry-type date, grown especially in Upper Egypt and the Western Desert oases, prized for an elongated fruit that ripens from lemon-yellow through orange to brown with a firmer, drier texture than Egypt's well-known soft dates. That dry texture gives Sakkoti dates an unusually long storage life without refrigeration, making them a traditional staple for year-round eating rather than a short fresh-market treat. Like other date palms it demands a long, intensely hot growing season, deep well-drained soil, and dependable pollination, with many years required before a young palm begins bearing. Give it generous permanent spacing to accommodate its eventual mature size.
sources: FAO Regional Office for the Near East — Date Palm Cultivars
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Date Palm Culture

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed well past the last frost into well-drained ground; this landrace tolerates heat and drought far better than ornamental or syrup sorghums and does not need irrigation once established.

directions: Feterita is a Sudanese grain sorghum landrace that arose from ancient natural crossing between Caudatum and Guinea sorghum races in Sudan's Nuba Mountains, and it remains a dietary staple there for porridge and flatbread. The plant has notably sparse foliage and slender, dry stalks topped by compact, oval grain heads bearing large, chalky-white seeds that distinguish it from bushier forage sorghums. Its deep rooting and tolerance of poor, erratic rainfall make it a reliable choice for low-input, drought-prone garden trials, though yields respond well to even modest supplemental moisture. Thin direct-sown seedlings to final spacing once established, and expect birds to show strong interest in the ripening grain heads.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) — Sorghum Genetic Resources
International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; protect young trees from any freezing temperatures.

directions: Ortanique is a natural orange-tangerine hybrid first identified in Jamaica's Manchester parish in the 1920s by grower David Daniel Phillips, who coined its name by blending 'orange,' 'tangerine,' and 'unique.' The fruit has a thick but easy-peeling rind over bright orange, juicy flesh with a distinctive sweet-tart balance that growers outside Jamaica's cool highland, bauxite-rich soils have struggled to fully replicate. Give it full sun, well-drained slightly acidic soil, and standard citrus feeding through the growing season, watering deeply but allowing the soil to dry somewhat between waterings. Harvest in winter into early spring once fruit colors fully and the rind loosens slightly, since Ortanique holds well on the tree without losing quality.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
